Name: zircon_network_plate_tectonics_onset
Title: Detecting the Onset of Global Plate Tectonics via Zircon Age Network Connectivity and Multi-Proxy Integration
Experiment: 1. Datasets: Compile all available detrital zircon U-Pb ages (ca. 3.5–1.8 Ga) from sedimentary rocks globally, with each sample tagged to its present-day craton and depositional age (time bins of 50 Myr). Additionally, assemble independent proxy datasets: mafic dyke swarm orientations (for crustal rigidity), metamorphic P–T–t paths (for thermal gradients), and paleomagnetic poles where available. 2. Metrics: Primary metric is inter-craton detrital zircon age similarity using a bootstrapped Kolmogorov-Smirnov D statistic transformed into a link weight. From the resulting networks, compute global efficiency, modularity, and within-cluster coherence. For each time slice, also calculate a 'plate-linkage probability' based on the fraction of craton pairs exceeding a similarity threshold. Independent proxies are scored for rigidity (dyke swarm parallelism) and metamorphic thermal gradient ratio. 3. Baseline comparisons: Compare observed network metrics against a null model where zircon ages are randomly shuffled among cratons preserving age distribution; also compare against the scaling behavior of a fully coupled model (modern plate tectonics) and a stagnant-lid model. Evaluate against published timelines for plate tectonic onset (e.g., 3.2 vs. 2.7 Ga). 4. Expected outcomes: A statistically significant increase in network connectivity and decrease in modularity (cohesive global network) at a specific time horizon, likely 3.0–2.8 Ga, coincident with rising rigidity indicators and a shift to lower-T/P metamorphism. The combined multi-proxy metric should show a sharp threshold rather than a gradual trend. 5. Ablation studies: Vary the time bin size (30, 50, 100 Myr), the similarity threshold, the minimum number of valid zircons per craton, and exclude individual cratons to test robustness. Re-run after randomly perturbing depositional ages within errors to assess sensitivity.
Abstract: The transition from local subduction to a globally interconnected system of rigid plates remains one of the most debated topics in Earth's early evolution. We present a quantitative, multi-proxy network framework that leverages global detrital zircon age spectra as an intermediary tracer of sediment dispersal and, by inference, plate connectivity. By constructing time-resolved networks among Archaean cratons and computing graph-theoretic measures of integration, we identify a statistically robust threshold in inter-craton age similarity between 3.0 and 2.8 Ga, indicative of the first sustained global plate linkages. The network signal aligns with independent proxies for crustal rigidity—dyke swarm parallelism and extensional basin geometries—and a coeval shift in metamorphic thermal regimes, validating the methodology. Geodynamic simulations of local versus global subduction regimes confirm that only a fully linked mobile-lid convection can reproduce the observed network topology. Our results provide the first quantitative, multi-proxy test for the emergence of global plate tectonics and constrain the timing to the Mesoarchaean, opening new avenues for reconstructing deep-time plate configurations.
Method: 1. Multi-Proxy Data Compilation and Segmentation: We partition the continental crust into genetically independent cratonic blocks (segmentation) and assemble for each a time series of detrital zircon U-Pb ages, metamorphic P–T–t estimates, mafic dyke swarm data, and sedimentary basin geometries. This allows each block’s tectonic behavior to be assessed in isolation before testing for interconnections. 2. Intermediary-Based Linkage Inference: Detrital zircons are treated as passive carriers (intermediary) of provenance information that can be spatially remobilized; we measure pairwise age spectrum similarity between cratons using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic over 50-Myr depositional windows. A statistically calibrated threshold converts this similarity into a binary link, creating an evolving network where edges denote probable fluvial or far-field sediment transport, and thus plate linkages. 3. Parameter-Space Exploration for Regime Detection: We systematically vary the link-formation threshold and the temporal resolution (parameter change) to define a stability field where a global, highly connected network emerges abruptly. Graph metrics—global efficiency, modularity, and clustering coefficient—quantify the degree to which the system transitions from isolated, high-modularity (local subduction) to integrated, low-modularity (global plate network) architectures. 4. Geodynamic Ground-Truthing and Multi-Proxy Synthesis: We run 3D spherical convection simulations with mobile and stagnant lids, incorporating passive tracers that mimic zircon production, erosion, and deposition. Model-generated age spectra are run through the same network pipeline, and the resulting topology is compared to the empirical record. Finally, we combine the normalized zircon-network score with independent rigidity and metamorphic proxies into a single ‘Global Plate Tectonics Index’ that sharply rises at the onset of mobile-lid behavior.
